days.title: Building Threat Detection and Alerting Pipelines

concepts.heading: Deriving Monitoring Requirements from Workloads
concepts.body: Before enabling any detection service, map what normal behavior looks like for a given workload: which accounts, regions, and resource types matter, what health checks already exist, and what business impact a compromise would cause. This analysis drives concrete decisions, such as which GuardDuty protection plans (EKS, RDS, Lambda, EBS malware protection) to turn on and which accounts need which Security Hub CSPM standards enabled (the original AWS Security Hub is now named AWS Security Hub CSPM). Skipping this step causes alert fatigue later, because everything gets monitored with the same sensitivity instead of being tuned to what actually matters for that workload.

concepts.heading: Amazon GuardDuty: Continuous Threat Detection
concepts.body: GuardDuty continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs, and CloudTrail management and S3 data events using threat intelligence feeds and machine learning, with no agents to deploy. It surfaces findings such as compromised credentials making unusual API calls, instances communicating with known command-and-control infrastructure, or cryptocurrency-mining behavior. A key exam nuance: GuardDuty is account- and region-scoped by default, so multi-account organizations designate a delegated administrator account to view findings from every member account in one place instead of managing each account separately.

concepts.heading: AWS Security Hub CSPM: Normalizing and Aggregating Findings
concepts.body: Security Hub CSPM ingests findings from GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer, and many partner tools, converting them to the AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF) so they can be compared and acted on consistently. It also runs its own standards checks, such as CIS AWS Foundations or the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard, and can trigger automated remediation through EventBridge rules. The exam trap is confusing Security Hub's aggregation role with GuardDuty's detection role: Security Hub does not analyze raw network traffic itself, it consolidates findings other services already generated.

concepts.heading: Amazon Macie: Discovering and Classifying Sensitive Data
concepts.body: Macie uses managed data identifiers, pattern matching, and machine learning to scan S3 buckets for sensitive data such as PII, PHI, and credentials, assigning each bucket a sensitivity score and publishing the results as findings. You can run one-time or scheduled discovery jobs, and results flow into Security Hub for a unified view alongside other findings. Macie is about classification, not intrusion detection, so a common wrong-answer pattern is selecting Macie for a question that is really about detecting attacker behavior, which is GuardDuty's job.

concepts.heading: Amazon Security Lake: A Normalized Data Lake for Security Telemetry
concepts.body: Security Lake automatically collects logs from AWS sources, including CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 resolver logs, and Security Hub findings, plus custom or third-party sources, converts them to the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF), and stores them in an S3-based data lake partitioned by account, region, and date. Subscribers, including third-party SIEM tools, can query the data directly or be notified of new arrivals. Unlike the finding-centric Security Hub, Security Lake is log-centric, making it the right answer whenever a requirement calls for long-term retention or feeding an external analytics pipeline.

concepts.heading: Automating Recurring Evaluation and Alerting
concepts.body: Beyond real-time detection, mature programs schedule recurring reviews: AWS Config conformance packs bundle rules that continuously check for compliance drift, Systems Manager State Manager runs periodic association documents to verify agent health or configuration state, and Security Hub can push summarized findings on a cadence through EventBridge to Slack, a ticketing system, or SNS. Building this automation early avoids depending on someone manually checking a dashboard, which the exam treats as an anti-pattern for production security operations.

examPoints: When a scenario describes wanting one normalized, cross-account view of findings that multiple security services already produced, that phrasing points to Security Hub; when it instead emphasizes a durable, queryable data lake of security logs feeding external tools, that points to Security Lake.

Read each answer choice for exactly what it detects: GuardDuty finds behavioral or network-based threats, Macie finds sensitive data at rest, and Inspector finds software vulnerabilities — exam questions frequently list all three as distractors for one another.

quiz.q: A security team manages 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and wants a single, normalized dashboard showing findings generated by GuardDuty, Macie, and Inspector across every account. Which service should they use?
quiz.explain: Security Hub CSPM aggregates and normalizes findings from GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, and other sources into ASFF for a unified cross-account dashboard. AWS Config only evaluates resource configuration compliance, and Trusted Advisor focuses on best-practice checks, not security findings aggregation.

quiz.q: A retail company must automatically discover and classify any customer PII that developers accidentally upload to shared S3 buckets. Which service directly addresses this requirement?
quiz.explain: Macie is purpose-built to scan S3 objects and classify sensitive data such as PII using machine learning and pattern matching. GuardDuty detects threat behavior rather than classifying data content, and Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not data sensitivity.

days.recap: Day 1 built the detection foundation: GuardDuty watches for threat behavior, Macie classifies sensitive data, Security Hub normalizes and aggregates findings from both, and Security Lake retains the underlying telemetry as an OCSF-formatted data lake.

days.title: Designing Centralized, Multi-Account Logging

concepts.heading: Matching Log Sources to Requirements
concepts.body: Every logging design starts by mapping a stated requirement to the log source that actually captures it: API activity needs CloudTrail, network-layer connections need VPC Flow Logs, DNS lookups need Route 53 Resolver query logs, and application behavior needs CloudWatch Logs from the CloudWatch agent or an embedded SDK. The exam frequently tests whether you pick the source that captures the exact signal described in the scenario, rather than a source that merely sounds security-related, so look for the specific artifact being asked about — an IP connection, a DNS query, or an IAM API call.

concepts.heading: Organization Trails for Centralized API Auditing
concepts.body: An AWS Organizations trail, created once from the management account, automatically applies to every current and future member account and cannot be disabled by a member account's own administrators, preventing a compromised or careless account from hiding its activity. Logs typically land in a dedicated log-archive account's S3 bucket protected by a restrictive bucket policy and, ideally, S3 Object Lock, so even the management account cannot tamper with historical data. This is the default answer whenever a scenario says every member account's API activity must be captured with no way to opt out.

concepts.heading: Security Lake for Cross-Source Log Normalization
concepts.body: Security Lake ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 resolver logs, and Security Hub CSPM findings automatically, normalizes them into OCSF, and stores them in a managed S3 data lake queryable with Athena or shareable with subscriber accounts and third-party tools. Choose it when a requirement calls for a durable, structured repository spanning many log types and accounts, not just routing raw logs to a bucket. Custom sources let on-premises or SaaS logs join the same OCSF-formatted lake alongside native AWS telemetry.

concepts.heading: Choosing Network-Layer Log Sources by Threat Type
concepts.body: VPC Flow Logs capture IP-level traffic metadata — source, destination, ports, accept or reject, byte counts — at the VPC, subnet, or ENI level, making them the go-to source for detecting port scanning, unusual egress, or traffic toward disallowed CIDR ranges. Transit Gateway Flow Logs extend that same visibility across a hub-and-spoke network. Route 53 Resolver query logs instead capture the DNS queries VPC resources make, which is the only way to catch DNS-based threats such as beaconing to a malicious domain, since Flow Logs record only the resolved IP, never the queried domain name.

concepts.heading: Routing and Retaining Logs Cost-Effectively
concepts.body: CloudWatch Logs suits near-real-time querying and alerting but becomes expensive at long retention windows, so long-term archives typically flow to S3, often via a subscription filter into Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose), with S3 Lifecycle rules moving older data into the S3 Glacier storage classes. Designing this pipeline correctly — CloudWatch for hot data, S3 and its Glacier storage classes for cold data, Security Lake for normalized cross-account analysis — is a recurring theme, and questions about reducing logging cost while meeting a multi-year retention requirement are testing exactly this trade-off.

examPoints: When a scenario says every member account's API activity must be captured centrally with no way for a member account to opt out, the organization trail feature of AWS CloudTrail is almost always the intended answer.

If the scenario describes detecting communication with a malicious domain name specifically, not just a malicious IP, the required log source is Route 53 Resolver query logs, not VPC Flow Logs, since Flow Logs only ever record resolved IP addresses and ports.

quiz.q: A company onboards new AWS accounts frequently and is worried a compromised member account's administrator could disable CloudTrail to hide malicious activity. What should they implement?
choices: A CloudTrail trail configured individually in each account
An AWS Organizations trail created from the management account
A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter in each account
An S3 bucket policy that blocks all deletes
quiz.explain: An organization trail is created once in the management account, applies to all member accounts automatically, and cannot be disabled by a member account's own administrator. Individual per-account trails can be turned off by a compromised account's administrator.

quiz.q: Security analysts suspect an EC2 instance is periodically resolving a known malicious domain name before establishing outbound connections. Which log source will show the actual domain name being queried?
quiz.explain: Route 53 Resolver query logs record the DNS query itself, including the requested domain name, which VPC Flow Logs cannot show since Flow Logs only capture the resolved IP address and port after the DNS lookup already completed.

days.recap: Day 2 focused on matching the right log source to the right signal: organization trails guarantee complete API visibility, Flow Logs and Resolver query logs cover different network layers, and Security Lake ties it all together in a normalized, queryable form.

days.title: Analyzing, Correlating, and Troubleshooting Logs

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Logs Insights for Near-Real-Time Queries
concepts.body: Logs Insights lets you run a purpose-built query language directly against CloudWatch Logs groups to filter, parse, and aggregate log events within seconds, which makes it ideal for investigating a live incident such as tracing every failed API call from a specific IAM principal in the last hour. It does not require any separate infrastructure or data movement, but its practicality drops for very large historical datasets spanning months, where cost and query time both grow, which is where Athena becomes the better tool.

concepts.heading: Amazon Athena for Large-Scale Historical Analysis
concepts.body: Athena runs standard SQL directly against data stored in S3 without requiring you to provision any servers, making it a cost-effective way to analyze large volumes of archived logs such as a year of CloudTrail or ALB access logs. Partitioning the S3 data by date and using a columnar format like Parquet dramatically reduces the amount of data scanned per query, which is what controls Athena's cost. The exam favors Athena whenever a scenario mentions large, already-archived log volumes and a need for ad hoc SQL analysis.

concepts.heading: Correlating Logs Across Sources with OpenSearch and Grafana
concepts.body: Amazon OpenSearch Service can ingest logs from many sources (via Lambda, Kinesis Data Firehose, or the OpenSearch ingestion pipeline), index them for full-text search, and support building dashboards that correlate events across systems, such as linking a suspicious login with subsequent API calls. Amazon Managed Grafana then visualizes metrics and logs from OpenSearch, CloudWatch, and other data sources side by side, which is useful when a security operations center needs one pane of glass spanning multiple telemetry systems rather than one log group at a time.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Why Monitoring Isn't Working
concepts.body: A large share of real-world 'my logs aren't showing up' problems trace back to IAM: the CloudWatch agent's instance profile lacking the logs:PutLogEvents permission, a Lambda execution role missing permissions to write to its log group, or a resource policy on a log group blocking a service principal. The systematic troubleshooting order is to check IAM permissions first, then the agent or service configuration (correct log group and stream names, correct region), and only then investigate the log group's retention or subscription settings — the exam rewards following this order rather than guessing.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Application and Infrastructure Resource Issues
concepts.body: Beyond logging pipelines themselves, monitoring gaps often originate in the monitored resource: a Lambda function missing the CloudWatch Logs permissions in its execution role, an API Gateway stage without access logging enabled, or a CloudFront distribution not configured to deliver logs to the expected S3 bucket. Recognizing that the root cause frequently sits in the resource's own configuration or permissions, not in CloudWatch itself, helps you eliminate wrong answers that only suggest changing alerting rules or dashboards.

examPoints: For cost-effective SQL analysis over a large volume of logs already archived in S3, Athena is almost always the preferred choice over scanning the same data with Logs Insights or a compute instance.

When a scenario says a specific log has stopped appearing in CloudWatch, check IAM permissions and agent or service configuration first, in that order, before assuming a CloudWatch-side setting like retention is the cause.

quiz.q: A company has multiple years of ALB access logs stored in S3 and needs to run occasional SQL queries to investigate historical traffic patterns without provisioning any servers. Which service best fits this need?
choices: AWS Lambda iterating over every log file
quiz.explain: Athena runs serverless SQL directly against data in S3, which is both cost-effective and requires no infrastructure for large historical log analysis. Iterating over files with Lambda or scanning with DynamoDB is far less efficient for this use case.

quiz.q: An engineer notices that a specific EC2 instance's logs have stopped appearing in CloudWatch Logs. What should be checked first?
choices: The CloudWatch agent configuration and its instance's IAM permissions
quiz.explain: The most common causes of missing logs are a misconfigured CloudWatch agent or missing IAM permissions to write log events, so these should be checked before unrelated settings like S3 lifecycle rules or networking.

days.recap: Day 3 distinguished tools by purpose — Logs Insights for near-real-time investigation, Athena for large-scale historical SQL analysis — and established a systematic troubleshooting order of permissions, then configuration, for missing logs.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: The Detection Pipeline End to End

concepts.heading: From Requirements to Detection Services
concepts.body: Domain 1 begins with analyzing a workload to derive monitoring requirements, then mapping those requirements onto GuardDuty for threat behavior, Macie for sensitive data classification, and Security Hub (now named Security Hub CSPM) for aggregating the resulting findings into one normalized view. The exam consistently rewards candidates who can identify exactly which of these three a scenario is describing, since the services sound similar but detect fundamentally different things — behavior, data content, and cross-service aggregation, respectively.

concepts.heading: From Collection to Centralization
concepts.body: The logging layer complements detection by capturing the raw evidence those services analyze: organization trails guarantee CloudTrail coverage across every account, VPC Flow Logs and Route 53 Resolver query logs cover different layers of network activity, and Security Lake normalizes everything into OCSF for long-term, cross-account, cross-tool analysis. Recognize that Security Hub is finding-centric while Security Lake is log-centric — a subtle distinction that the exam uses to separate two otherwise similar-sounding centralization services.

concepts.heading: From Data to Insight: Analysis and Troubleshooting
concepts.body: Once logs are collected, CloudWatch Logs Insights supports fast, near-real-time investigation while Athena handles large-scale historical SQL analysis over archived data in S3, and OpenSearch with Managed Grafana adds full-text search and cross-source dashboards for a security operations center. When logs seem to be missing entirely, the reflex should be to check IAM permissions and service configuration before assuming the pipeline itself is broken.

concepts.heading: Weighing the Domain Correctly
concepts.body: Detection carries 16% of the exam, meaning it will not dominate the test, but its concepts (what each service detects, and how logs flow into that detection) resurface indirectly throughout Incident Response and Infrastructure Security questions later in the exam. A candidate who cannot instantly distinguish GuardDuty from Macie from Security Hub will lose points not just in this domain but in scenario questions elsewhere that reference these services in passing.

examPoints: When a question tests 'which service does X,' first identify whether X is detecting a threat, classifying data, aggregating findings, or storing normalized logs — each maps to exactly one of GuardDuty, Macie, Security Hub, or Security Lake.

quiz.q: What core competency does Domain 1 (Detection) primarily test?
choices: Building monitoring, logging, and analysis capability to detect security events
quiz.explain: Detection covers designing, implementing, and troubleshooting the monitoring and logging systems used to detect threats and anomalies. Network topology, IAM policy authoring, and cost optimization are covered elsewhere or not at all on this exam.

quiz.q: A company wants a normalized, long-term data lake of security logs from AWS and third-party sources that external analytics tools can query. Which service fits this need?
quiz.explain: Security Lake normalizes logs from AWS and custom or third-party sources into OCSF and stores them in a queryable S3-based data lake designed for exactly this purpose. The other services address configuration compliance, identity management, and backup, not log centralization.

days.recap: Day 4 closed the loop on Detection: identify what needs monitoring, collect the right logs, route them into GuardDuty, Macie, and Security Hub for detection, and use Athena or Logs Insights to investigate — the full detection pipeline from raw signal to actionable finding.

days.title: Designing and Testing Incident Response Plans

concepts.heading: Writing Runbooks for Security Incidents
concepts.body: A runbook translates an incident type — credential compromise, data exfiltration, a DDoS event — into a concrete, ordered set of steps a responder can follow under pressure, rather than improvising. Systems Manager OpsCenter centralizes operational items (OpsItems) tied to a specific incident, linking related CloudWatch alarms, Config rule violations, and runbook automation documents so responders have one place to work from. Well-written runbooks specify exactly which AWS API calls or console actions to take at each step, minimizing decision-making time during a live incident.

concepts.heading: Preparing in Advance: Access, Tooling, and Blast Radius
concepts.body: Incident preparation means provisioning break-glass access roles before they're needed, pre-deploying forensic tooling (like a dedicated forensics VPC with EC2 for evidence analysis), and designing account and network boundaries so a single compromised resource cannot reach everything else — this is what 'minimizing blast radius' means in practice, achieved through account separation, least-privilege IAM, and network segmentation. AWS Shield Advanced also belongs in preparation: subscribing in advance, not during an active DDoS event, is what unlocks 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) and cost protection for scaling caused by an attack.

concepts.heading: Validating Response Plans Without Causing Real Outages
concepts.body: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) runs controlled experiments — terminating an instance, injecting latency, throttling an API — against real infrastructure in a safe, scoped, and reversible way, which lets teams verify that their monitoring actually fires and their runbooks actually work before a real incident forces the test. AWS Resilience Hub complements this by assessing an application's architecture against a defined resiliency policy and recommending changes, focusing more on recoverability (RTO/RPO) than on active security incident response, but the two are often paired in exam scenarios about validating readiness.

concepts.heading: Matching Runbooks to Incident Categories
concepts.body: Different incident types demand materially different first steps: a leaked IAM access key calls for immediate key deactivation and CloudTrail review of everything that key touched, a suspected data exfiltration event calls for network isolation and reviewing S3 access logs or VPC Flow Logs for the destination, and a DDoS event calls for engaging Shield Advanced and the DRT rather than manual scaling. Building a distinct runbook per category, instead of one generic 'security incident' runbook, is what the exam expects a mature program to do.

examPoints: When a scenario asks how to verify an incident response plan actually works without causing a real outage, AWS Fault Injection Service's controlled chaos experiments are the intended mechanism, not a tabletop exercise alone.

Remember that Shield Advanced's DRT support and cost protection only apply if you subscribed before the attack; a scenario about scrambling to enable protection during an active DDoS event is testing whether you know that preparation must happen ahead of time.

quiz.q: A company wants to verify, without causing a real production outage, that its incident response runbooks and monitoring alarms actually trigger correctly during a simulated failure. Which service should they use?
quiz.explain: FIS runs controlled, scoped experiments that simulate real failure conditions to validate resilience and incident response readiness. Config, Inspector, and Trusted Advisor evaluate configuration and compliance but do not simulate failures.

quiz.q: What does 'minimizing blast radius' mean in the context of incident response preparation?
choices: Consolidating all workloads into a single account for simplicity
Designing account, network, and permission boundaries so a compromise in one area cannot easily spread to others
Collecting the maximum possible amount of logging
Minimizing AWS spend across all accounts
quiz.explain: Blast radius minimization is achieved through account separation, least-privilege IAM, and network segmentation so that a breach in one area is contained rather than spreading. Consolidating everything into one account would increase, not decrease, blast radius.

days.recap: Designing incident response starts with runbooks and blast-radius-minimizing preparation, then uses FIS and Resilience Hub to validate that both the plan and the infrastructure will actually hold up before a real incident occurs.

days.title: Automating Incident Response with Orchestration

concepts.heading: Systems Manager Automation for Standardized Response Actions
concepts.body: SSM Automation runs predefined documents (runbooks encoded as executable automation) that perform standardized actions like isolating an instance by swapping its security group, taking an EBS snapshot for forensic preservation, or tagging a resource for investigation, all without a human manually clicking through the console. Automation documents can be triggered manually, on a schedule, or in response to an EventBridge event such as a new GuardDuty finding, which is what turns detection into response without waiting for an on-call engineer to wake up.

concepts.heading: Automated Forensics Orchestration for Compromised Instances
concepts.body: The Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2 solution (built on Step Functions and SSM Automation) responds to a GuardDuty finding by automatically isolating the suspected instance, capturing a memory dump and EBS snapshot for evidence, and tagging the case for investigators, all while preserving a chain of custody. This is the specific answer whenever a scenario emphasizes both speed and forensic integrity — capturing evidence before an attacker can cover their tracks or before an automated termination destroys volatile evidence like memory contents.

concepts.heading: Orchestrating Multi-Step Response with Step Functions
concepts.body: AWS Step Functions models an incident response process as an explicit state machine, calling Lambda functions, SSM Automation documents, and other AWS APIs in a defined sequence with built-in error handling, retries, and parallel branches — for example, isolate the instance, then in parallel notify the security team and start log collection, then wait for analyst approval before terminating. Step Functions is preferred over a single large Lambda function whenever the workflow has multiple ordered or conditional stages spanning several services, since it provides visibility into exactly which step failed.

concepts.heading: Automating Recovery Alongside Response
concepts.body: Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) manages multi-region failover through routing controls and Region switch plans (the older readiness check feature has been closed to new customers since 2026-04-30; Region switch plan evaluation now covers readiness), which would be invoked as part of a broader incident response workflow when an incident (such as a regional compromise or an availability-impacting attack) requires shifting traffic away from an affected region. While ARC is more of a resilience tool than a pure security tool, the exam pairs it with incident automation when a scenario needs both containment and continued availability during the response.

examPoints: When a scenario emphasizes automatically collecting forensic evidence (memory, disk) from a suspected instance while preserving chain of custody, Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2 is the specific, named solution being tested.

Choose Step Functions over a single Lambda function whenever the described workflow has multiple ordered or conditional steps across different services — the exam signals this with phrases like 'first... then... if approved...'.

quiz.q: Which AWS solution automatically collects memory and disk forensic evidence from an EC2 instance suspected of compromise while preserving a defensible chain of custody?
choices: Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2
quiz.explain: Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2 automates snapshotting, memory capture, and evidence tagging with chain-of-custody preservation for compromised instances. AWS Backup only performs generic backups and has no forensic evidence-handling capability.

quiz.q: An incident response workflow needs to isolate a compromised instance, then run two tasks in parallel (notify the security team and begin log collection), and only proceed to termination after analyst approval. Which service best orchestrates this?
quiz.explain: Step Functions is designed for exactly this kind of ordered, conditional, parallel multi-step orchestration with built-in state visibility. S3, Direct Connect, and Route 53 are storage and networking services with no workflow orchestration capability.

days.recap: Automated response combines SSM Automation for standardized actions, the Forensics Orchestrator for evidence preservation, and Step Functions for orchestrating multi-service workflows, turning detection into fast, consistent containment.

days.title: Responding to Active Security Events

concepts.heading: Capturing and Preserving Evidence
concepts.body: The moment an incident is confirmed, the priority shifts to preserving evidence before it is lost or altered: taking EBS snapshots of affected volumes, exporting relevant CloudWatch Logs and CloudTrail events to a write-once S3 location (ideally with Object Lock enabled), and avoiding actions that would overwrite volatile data such as rebooting a compromised instance before capturing memory. Evidence handling procedures should be defined in the runbook ahead of time so no one has to improvise chain-of-custody decisions mid-incident.

concepts.heading: Correlating Findings and Logs Across Services
concepts.body: A real incident rarely shows up as a single finding; it appears as a GuardDuty alert, a related set of unusual CloudTrail API calls, and a spike in VPC Flow Logs traffic that must be pieced together to understand the true scope. Amazon Detective automatically extracts this behavioral data and builds a graph model linking findings, IP addresses, IAM principals, and API calls over time, letting an investigator visually trace how an incident unfolded instead of manually cross-referencing raw logs across multiple consoles.

concepts.heading: Validating Findings and Scoping Impact
concepts.body: Not every finding indicates a genuine compromise, so investigators validate findings by checking whether the flagged behavior matches known-legitimate activity (a scheduled batch job, an approved penetration test) before committing response resources, and then scope the impact by identifying every resource, credential, and data store the compromised identity or instance could have touched. Detective's timeline and finding-group features both help establish this scope quickly by showing related activity rather than a single isolated event.

concepts.heading: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery
concepts.body: The three classic incident response phases map to concrete AWS actions: containment isolates the affected resource, typically by swapping its security group to deny all traffic or revoking its IAM credentials; eradication removes the root cause, such as deleting a malicious IAM user, rotating all credentials the attacker touched, or patching the exploited vulnerability; and recovery restores normal operation, often by launching a clean replacement instance from a hardened AMI or restoring data from an AWS Backup recovery point known to predate the compromise.

concepts.heading: Root Cause Analysis with Amazon Detective
concepts.body: After containment, Detective's automatically maintained behavior graph supports root cause analysis by letting analysts pivot from a finding to related entities — for example, from a suspicious IP to every IAM principal that communicated with it, and from there to every API call each principal made — without writing custom log queries. This dramatically reduces investigation time compared to manually correlating GuardDuty findings with raw CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log data, which is the capability the exam is testing when a scenario asks for fast root-cause determination across multiple data sources.

examPoints: When a scenario describes needing to connect several findings and multiple log sources into one coherent picture of an attack's timeline, Amazon Detective's graph-based analysis is the intended answer, not manually querying CloudTrail.

Keep the three response phases distinct in your mind: containment isolates, eradication removes the root cause, and recovery restores normal service — the exam often asks which phase a specific described action belongs to.

quiz.q: Which service automatically links GuardDuty findings, VPC Flow Logs, and CloudTrail events into a graph to accelerate root cause analysis of a security event?
quiz.explain: Detective automatically extracts and links behavioral data from multiple sources into a visual graph purpose-built for investigation and root cause analysis. Config, Trusted Advisor, and Macie serve compliance, best-practice, and data classification purposes respectively, not incident correlation.

quiz.q: During incident response, which phase involves isolating a compromised resource from the network to prevent the incident from spreading further?
quiz.explain: Containment is specifically about isolating affected resources to stop further spread, distinct from eradication (removing the root cause) and recovery (restoring normal operation).

days.recap: Responding to an active event means preserving evidence, using Detective to correlate findings and logs into a full timeline, validating scope, and then working through containment, eradication, and recovery in that order.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Preparation, Automation, and Response

concepts.heading: Two Axes: Before and During an Incident
concepts.body: Domain 2 splits cleanly into preparation (runbooks, blast-radius-minimizing design, FIS-validated readiness) and active response (containment, eradication, recovery, powered by Detective for correlation). A useful first filter for any Domain 2 question is deciding whether the scenario describes something happening before an incident (planning, testing) or during one (an active compromise requiring immediate action), since that determines which half of the service list is relevant.

concepts.heading: Automation as the Bridge Between the Two
concepts.body: SSM Automation, the Forensics Orchestrator, and Step Functions sit between preparation and response: they are built and tested during preparation but execute automatically during a real incident, converting a detection (a GuardDuty finding) into an immediate, consistent, human-independent action such as isolating an instance and preserving its evidence. Recognizing this bridging role helps place automation questions correctly rather than filing them under either preparation or response exclusively.

concepts.heading: Evidence Integrity Throughout the Lifecycle
concepts.body: Whether captured manually or via the Forensics Orchestrator, evidence handling threads through the entire domain: snapshots and logs must be preserved before remediation actions like termination destroy them, and stored in a way (such as S3 with Object Lock) that maintains a defensible chain of custody. Exam questions that mention 'preserve evidence' or 'chain of custody' are testing whether you sequence evidence capture before destructive remediation steps.

concepts.heading: Weighing the Domain Correctly
concepts.body: Incident Response carries 14% of the exam and is tightly connected to Domain 1 (which supplies the findings and logs Domain 2 acts on) and Domain 3 (whose network and compute controls are what containment actually manipulates). Treat these three domains as one continuous pipeline — detect, decide, contain — rather than three unrelated topics, since many scenario questions blend elements from all three.

examPoints: A Domain 2 question is almost always testing either 'is this preparation or active response' or 'which of containment, eradication, or recovery does this action represent' — identify which framing applies before picking an answer.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT part of incident response preparation?
choices: Testing the response plan with AWS Fault Injection Service
quiz.explain: Isolating an actively compromised instance is a containment action taken during a real incident, while the other three options are all preparation activities performed before an incident occurs.

quiz.q: Which service is responsible for orchestrating a sequential, multi-service incident response workflow with conditional branches and built-in error handling?
quiz.explain: Step Functions is purpose-built for orchestrating exactly this kind of ordered, conditional, multi-service workflow, which incident response often requires. CloudFront, Direct Connect, and RDS have no workflow orchestration role.

days.recap: Domain 2 closes the loop from planning (runbooks, blast radius, FIS validation) through automated action (SSM Automation, Step Functions, Forensics Orchestrator) to full containment, eradication, recovery, and root-cause analysis with Detective.

days.title: Securing the Network Edge

concepts.heading: Threat-Modeling the Edge
concepts.body: Edge security design starts by cataloging the threats a public-facing application actually faces: OWASP Top 10 web application attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, volumetric and protocol DDoS attacks, credential-stuffing bots, and cross-origin data leakage. Each threat category maps to a distinct AWS control, so a well-designed edge strategy is rarely a single service — it is CloudFront for content delivery and basic protection, WAF for application-layer filtering, and Shield Advanced for DDoS-specific defense, layered together.

concepts.heading: AWS WAF: Application-Layer Filtering
concepts.body: WAF evaluates HTTP/HTTPS requests against rules attached to a CloudFront distribution, ALB, API Gateway, or AppSync API, and includes AWS Managed Rule Groups for common threats (SQL injection, known bad inputs, bot control) as well as custom rules. Two rule types recur constantly on the exam: Geo Match rules block or allow traffic by the request's geographic origin, and rate-based rules automatically block a source IP once its request rate within a rolling time window exceeds a defined threshold, which is the standard defense against credential-stuffing and brute-force login attempts.

concepts.heading: AWS Shield Advanced for DDoS Protection
concepts.body: Shield Standard is automatically included for all AWS customers and defends against common, most-frequent network and transport layer DDoS attacks at no extra cost, while Shield Advanced is a paid subscription adding enhanced detection for larger and more sophisticated attacks, near-real-time visibility, integration with WAF for automatic rule creation during an attack, cost protection against usage spikes caused by the attack, and 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team. Advanced only delivers these benefits for resources associated with it before an attack begins.

concepts.heading: Securing Cross-Origin Requests and Headers
concepts.body: S3's CORS configuration controls which origins, methods, and headers a browser is allowed to use when a web page hosted elsewhere makes requests to an S3 bucket, preventing malicious sites from silently reading data intended only for a specific trusted origin. CloudFront response headers policies can add security headers (like Content-Security-Policy or Strict-Transport-Security) at the edge without modifying origin application code, which is a fast way to harden many applications behind one distribution simultaneously.

examPoints: When a scenario requires blocking traffic from specific countries at the application layer, WAF's Geo Match rule is the answer; when it requires network- or transport-layer blocking (like a security group), Geo Match is not applicable since WAF operates at layer 7.

For repeated failed login attempts or credential-stuffing from the same IP within a short window, WAF's rate-based rule type is the specific feature being tested, distinct from a static IP set rule that blocks a fixed list of addresses.

quiz.q: An application needs to block HTTP requests originating from a specific set of countries at the application layer, before they reach the origin server. What should be configured?
choices: An AWS WAF Geo Match rule
quiz.explain: WAF's Geo Match rule filters requests based on geographic origin at the application layer. Security groups and NACLs operate on IP addresses and ports, not geography, and Route 53 health checks have no filtering role.

quiz.q: An application is experiencing credential-stuffing attacks where the same small set of IPs sends hundreds of login requests per minute. Which WAF rule type is designed to automatically block this pattern?
choices: IP set rule with a static list
quiz.explain: A rate-based rule automatically blocks a source IP once its request rate exceeds a configured threshold within a rolling time window, which is exactly the credential-stuffing pattern described. A static IP set requires knowing the IPs in advance and does not adapt automatically.

days.recap: Edge security layers WAF for application-layer filtering, Shield Advanced for DDoS defense (only effective if subscribed in advance), and CORS/response header policies for controlling cross-origin behavior and hardening headers at the edge.

days.title: Compute Workload Security I: Hardening and Vulnerability Scanning

concepts.heading: Building Hardened Images with a Repeatable Pipeline
concepts.body: EC2 Image Builder automates the process of building, testing, and distributing hardened AMIs and container images through a defined pipeline of components — installing security agents, applying CIS or STIG hardening benchmarks, running vulnerability tests — so every new image starts from the same known-good baseline instead of an ad hoc manual process. Pipelines can run on a schedule to automatically rebuild images whenever a base image is updated, ensuring newly launched instances never start from stale, unpatched software.

concepts.heading: Applying the Right IAM Role for the Job
concepts.body: Compute workloads need carefully scoped identities: an EC2 instance profile grants the permissions an application running on that instance needs, a Lambda execution role grants what that specific function needs, and a service-linked role grants a specific AWS service the permissions it needs to manage resources on your behalf. Reusing an overly broad role across many different workloads (for convenience) is a common anti-pattern the exam expects you to identify and correct with narrower, workload-specific roles.

concepts.heading: Vulnerability Scanning with Amazon Inspector
concepts.body: Inspector continuously scans EC2 instances, container images stored in ECR, and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and, for EC2, also evaluates network reachability to flag unintended exposure, all without requiring a scheduled scan window since it triggers automatically on relevant changes like a new package installation or image push. Inspector's job is to find known vulnerabilities in existing software, which distinguishes it from GuardDuty, whose job is to detect suspicious runtime behavior regardless of whether a known CVE is involved.

concepts.heading: Runtime Threat Detection for Compute
concepts.body: GuardDuty's Runtime Monitoring extends threat detection into the operating system and container runtime, observing process activity, file access, and network connections on EC2 instances, ECS tasks, and EKS pods to catch active exploitation, malware execution, or container escape attempts as they happen, rather than only flagging that a vulnerable package exists. Pairing Inspector's vulnerability scanning with GuardDuty's Runtime Monitoring is the standard 'defense in depth' pattern the exam expects for compute workloads — one finds the weakness, the other catches active exploitation of it.

examPoints: When a scenario asks for standardized, continuously updated, hardened AMIs built on a repeatable pipeline, EC2 Image Builder is the intended answer rather than manually patching and re-imaging instances.

Distinguish Inspector (finds known vulnerabilities in software that exists, whether or not it's being actively exploited) from GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring (detects active, suspicious runtime behavior) — exam distractors frequently swap these two.

quiz.q: Which service continuously scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions for known CVE vulnerabilities?
quiz.explain: Inspector automatically and continuously scans EC2, ECR images, and Lambda functions for known vulnerabilities. Config checks configuration compliance, Macie classifies sensitive data, and neither performs CVE scanning.

quiz.q: Which service builds and maintains a repeatable, automated pipeline for producing standardized, hardened AMIs and container images?
quiz.explain: EC2 Image Builder automates the pipeline of building, testing, hardening, and distributing AMIs and container images. Backup, S3, and Direct Connect play no role in image creation or hardening.

days.recap: Compute security starts with hardened, pipeline-built images and correctly scoped IAM roles, then layers Inspector's vulnerability scanning with GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring's behavioral detection for defense in depth.

days.title: Compute Workload Security II: Patching, Access, and Pipeline Security

concepts.heading: Automating Patch Deployment at Scale
concepts.body: Systems Manager Patch Manager automates scanning for and installing operating system and application patches across large fleets of instances based on defined patch baselines and maintenance windows, and can report on patch compliance across an entire organization through integration with Config. Pairing Patch Manager's remediation with Inspector's vulnerability findings closes the loop: Inspector tells you what's vulnerable, and Patch Manager fixes it on a controlled schedule instead of requiring manual, per-instance patching.

concepts.heading: Eliminating SSH Keys and Bastion Hosts with Session Manager
concepts.body: Session Manager provides browser- or CLI-based shell access to EC2 instances (and on-premises servers) using IAM permissions for authorization, without requiring any inbound ports to be open, an SSH key to be managed, or a bastion host to be maintained, and every session is logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for auditing. This directly eliminates two long-standing operational risks: leaked SSH keys and internet-facing bastion hosts as an attack surface, making it the default answer whenever a scenario asks how to reduce that specific attack surface.

concepts.heading: EC2 Instance Connect as a Complementary Option
concepts.body: EC2 Instance Connect pushes short-lived, one-time-use SSH public keys to an instance via IAM-authorized API calls, giving you the auditability and short-lived nature security teams want while still supporting workflows that specifically need a traditional SSH client rather than the Session Manager plugin. It solves a similar problem to Session Manager (removing the need to store and manage long-lived SSH keys) but is typically chosen when an existing SSH-based workflow needs the least disruptive fix.

concepts.heading: Finding and Fixing Vulnerabilities in the CI/CD Pipeline
concepts.body: Amazon Inspector code security scans application source code (SAST), third-party dependencies (SCA), and IaC templates in connected GitHub or GitLab repositories on push, on pull request, within CI/CD pipelines, or on a schedule, flagging security vulnerabilities and insecure patterns with remediation guidance rather than just a generic vulnerability list, which shifts security left into the development process instead of catching problems only after deployment. Combined with Amazon Q Developer code reviews for AI-assisted secure coding suggestions in the IDE, this represents the 'shift-left' pattern the exam expects for modern software delivery pipelines. (Older material names Amazon CodeGuru Security here; it was discontinued on 2025-11-20.)

examPoints: When a requirement says administrators must reach EC2 instances without opening inbound SSH ports or managing a bastion host, Systems Manager Session Manager is the standard answer, distinguished from EC2 Instance Connect by not requiring an SSH client at all.

For finding and fixing security vulnerabilities in source code and IaC before deployment, Amazon Inspector code security (or Amazon Q Developer code reviews in the IDE) is the current named service, since CodeGuru Security was discontinued on 2025-11-20; recognize 'shift-left' code scanning as distinct from Inspector's scanning of deployed EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions.

quiz.q: A security team wants engineers to access EC2 instances for troubleshooting without opening any inbound SSH port and without maintaining a bastion host. What should they implement?
choices: A security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22
Direct public IP assignment to every instance
quiz.explain: Session Manager provides IAM-authorized shell access with no inbound ports required and no bastion host to maintain. The other options all either open unnecessary network exposure or require infrastructure Session Manager eliminates.

quiz.q: Which service scans application source code within a CI/CD pipeline to automatically find and suggest fixes for security vulnerabilities before deployment?
quiz.explain: Amazon Inspector code security scans source code, dependencies, and IaC for vulnerabilities and provides remediation guidance as part of the pipeline. CodePipeline alone only orchestrates pipeline stages without performing security analysis, and S3 and Direct Connect are unrelated.

days.recap: Compute security continues with automated patching via Patch Manager, secure administrative access via Session Manager without SSH keys or bastions, and shift-left vulnerability scanning in the CI/CD pipeline with Amazon Inspector code security.

days.title: Designing Network Security Controls

concepts.heading: Layered Traffic Filtering with Security Groups and NACLs
concepts.body: Security groups are stateful and attached to ENIs, evaluating all rules together and automatically allowing return traffic for any allowed connection, while network ACLs are stateless, attached to subnets, evaluated in numbered rule order, and require explicit rules for both inbound and outbound (including ephemeral return-traffic ports). A common exam trap is forgetting NACL statelessness — allowing inbound traffic on a NACL without a matching outbound rule for the response will silently break connectivity, which is a frequent troubleshooting scenario.

concepts.heading: Deep Packet Inspection with AWS Network Firewall
concepts.body: AWS Network Firewall provides stateful, signature-based, and domain-based filtering at the VPC level, supporting features security groups and NACLs cannot, such as intrusion prevention signatures, TLS inspection, and outbound domain allow-lists, making it the right choice when a requirement goes beyond simple IP/port filtering into detecting or blocking known attack patterns or enforcing which external domains a VPC can reach. It's typically deployed in a centralized inspection VPC that other VPCs route through via Transit Gateway.

concepts.heading: Zero Trust Application Access with AWS Verified Access
concepts.body: AWS Verified Access replaces traditional VPN-based access to internal applications with a zero-trust model that evaluates identity (via an external IdP) and device posture (via an endpoint security signal) on every single request, granting or denying access without ever placing the client on the corporate network. This is the specific answer whenever a scenario wants to eliminate VPN client software while still enforcing conditional, continuously evaluated access to a private application, as opposed to a one-time login that grants broad network access.

concepts.heading: Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Connectivity Security
concepts.body: Site-to-Site VPN encrypts traffic over the public internet between on-premises networks and a VPC using IPsec, while Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private physical network connection that bypasses the public internet entirely (and can be combined with MACsec for link-layer encryption on the dedicated connection itself). Choosing between them depends on whether the requirement is encryption over an existing internet path (VPN, faster to provision) or a dedicated, consistent-latency private link (Direct Connect, better for predictable bandwidth and lower latency, plus MACsec if data must be encrypted in transit over that link too).

concepts.heading: Finding Unintended Network Paths
concepts.body: AWS Network Access Analyzer lets you define network access requirements (for example, 'no instance in this subnet should be reachable from the internet') and then automatically identifies any actual paths that violate those requirements by analyzing the effective combination of route tables, security groups, and NACLs. This is distinct from Inspector's network reachability findings, which surface exposure at the individual instance level; Network Access Analyzer is designed for broader, requirement-driven path analysis across the VPC.

examPoints: When a scenario wants to eliminate VPN client software while still enforcing per-request identity and device-posture checks for a private application, AWS Verified Access is the intended answer, not Client VPN or Site-to-Site VPN.

Remember that NACLs are stateless and security groups are stateful — a connectivity troubleshooting scenario that works with security groups configured correctly but still fails often points to a missing NACL outbound rule for ephemeral ports.

quiz.q: Which service allows access to a private application based on IdP authentication and device trust policies, without requiring a VPN client?
quiz.explain: Verified Access implements zero-trust access to private applications based on identity and device posture with no VPN client required. Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect both require establishing network-level connectivity rather than per-request identity checks.

quiz.q: Which tool proactively identifies unintended network paths or overly permissive access within a VPC based on defined access requirements?
quiz.explain: Network Access Analyzer evaluates route tables, security groups, and NACLs against defined access requirements to surface unintended paths. Backup, S3 Lifecycle, and Budgets have no network path analysis capability.

days.recap: Network security control design layers stateful security groups, stateless NACLs, deep-packet-inspecting Network Firewall, and zero-trust Verified Access, with Network Access Analyzer catching unintended paths across the whole stack.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Edge, Compute, and Network Layers

concepts.heading: The Three Layers of Infrastructure Security
concepts.body: Domain 3 organizes cleanly into three layers moving inward from the internet: the edge (CloudFront, WAF, Shield Advanced, defending against application-layer and DDoS attacks), compute (Image Builder, Inspector, GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring, Session Manager, defending the instances and containers themselves), and network (security groups, NACLs, Network Firewall, Verified Access, controlling traffic flow between and within VPCs). Recognizing which layer a scenario is describing is the fastest way to narrow four answer choices down to one or two plausible services.

concepts.heading: Recurring Cross-Layer Patterns
concepts.body: Two patterns repeat across all three layers: pairing a preventive control with a detective one (WAF prevents at the edge while GuardDuty detects; Patch Manager prevents at compute while Inspector detects vulnerabilities before they're exploited), and eliminating standing access in favor of just-in-time, identity-based access (Session Manager for instance access, Verified Access for application access) instead of always-open ports or persistent VPN tunnels.

concepts.heading: Zero Trust as the Connecting Theme
concepts.body: Both Session Manager (no SSH keys, no bastion, IAM-authorized) and Verified Access (no VPN, per-request identity and device checks) reflect the same zero-trust philosophy applied at different layers — access is granted based on verified identity and context for each specific request, not because a device happens to be on a particular network. Expect the exam to test whether you can identify this shared philosophy even when the specific service named differs.

concepts.heading: Weighing the Domain Correctly
concepts.body: Infrastructure Security carries 18% of the exam, the second-largest domain, reflecting how much of real-world AWS security work involves configuring these layered controls correctly. Investing extra review time here, particularly on the differences between overlapping tools (WAF vs. Shield, Session Manager vs. Instance Connect, security groups vs. NACLs), pays off disproportionately given the domain's weight.

examPoints: When a Domain 3 scenario is ambiguous, first identify the layer (edge, compute, or network) it describes, since narrowing to the right layer alone eliminates roughly two-thirds of a typical four-option question.

quiz.q: What are the three layers Domain 3 (Infrastructure Security) organizes around?
quiz.explain: Infrastructure Security is organized around the network edge, compute workloads, and network security controls, moving from the internet-facing boundary inward.

quiz.q: Which pair of services both implement a zero-trust, no-standing-access philosophy but at different layers?
quiz.explain: Verified Access (application access) and Session Manager (instance access) both grant access based on verified identity for each request rather than persistent network-level access, reflecting the same zero-trust principle at different layers.

days.recap: Domain 3 closes with a layered view: block attacks at the edge (WAF/Shield), harden and patch compute (Image Builder/Patch Manager), and defend the network with multiple overlapping controls (security groups/NACLs/Network Firewall/Verified Access).

days.title: Designing Authentication Strategies

concepts.heading: Separating Workforce Identity from Customer Identity
concepts.body: The single most important distinction in Domain 4 is between workforce identity (employees who need access to AWS accounts and internal tools) and customer identity (end users of an application you build), because AWS provides a purpose-built service for each: IAM Identity Center for the former, Amazon Cognito for the latter. Answering a question correctly almost always starts with identifying which of these two populations the scenario describes, since the two services are not interchangeable despite both handling 'authentication.'

concepts.heading: IAM Identity Center for Workforce SSO
concepts.body: IAM Identity Center provides a single sign-on experience across every AWS account in an AWS Organizations structure, letting a user log in once and access multiple accounts through permission sets that map to IAM roles created automatically in each target account. It supports its own built-in identity store or federation with an external identity provider via SAML or, for directory-based organizations, integration with AWS Directory Service or an existing on-premises Active Directory, avoiding duplicate identity management across dozens of accounts.

concepts.heading: Amazon Cognito for Customer-Facing Applications
concepts.body: Cognito provides user pools for sign-up, sign-in, and user directory management (including social identity provider federation like Google or Facebook, and enterprise federation via SAML/OIDC) plus identity pools for issuing temporary AWS credentials to authenticated or even unauthenticated app users so they can directly call AWS services like S3. This is the correct choice whenever a scenario describes end users of a mobile or web application, not employees managing AWS infrastructure.

concepts.heading: Enforcing Multi-Factor Authentication and External IdP Federation
concepts.body: MFA should be enforced as close to mandatory as possible for any human identity with console or API access, and both IAM Identity Center and Cognito support requiring it, along with IAM's own MFA enforcement via condition keys in policies (such as requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent). Federating with an external IdP (Okta, Azure AD, or an on-premises SAML/OIDC provider) centralizes identity lifecycle management (onboarding, offboarding, password policy) in the organization's existing system of record instead of duplicating it inside AWS.

examPoints: Distinguish workforce access (employees needing SSO across many AWS accounts) from customer access (end users of an application) immediately — the former points to IAM Identity Center, the latter to Cognito, and mixing them up is the most common wrong answer in this domain.

When a scenario mentions integrating with an existing on-premises Active Directory for workforce access, expect the answer to combine AWS Directory Service with IAM Identity Center rather than trying to force Cognito into a workforce use case.

quiz.q: A mobile application needs to let end customers sign up, log in (including via Google social login), and then directly upload files to an S3 bucket using temporary credentials. Which service should be used?
quiz.explain: Cognito is purpose-built for customer-facing applications, providing sign-up/sign-in, social identity federation, and temporary AWS credentials via identity pools. IAM Identity Center is designed for workforce access to AWS accounts, not application end users.

quiz.q: A company wants employees to sign in once and get SSO access to over 50 AWS accounts within their AWS Organizations structure. Which service provides this?
quiz.explain: IAM Identity Center provides centralized SSO with permission sets mapped to roles across every account in an organization. Cognito addresses customer-facing application identity, not workforce access to AWS accounts.

days.recap: Authentication strategy hinges on the workforce-versus-customer distinction: IAM Identity Center handles employee SSO across AWS accounts, while Cognito handles end-user sign-up, sign-in, and temporary credentials for applications.

days.title: Temporary Credentials and Authentication Troubleshooting

concepts.heading: Why Temporary Credentials Beat Long-Lived Keys
concepts.body: AWS STS issues temporary security credentials (an access key, secret key, and session token) with a defined expiration, typically through AssumeRole, that grant only the permissions of the assumed role for a limited window, dramatically reducing the damage a leaked credential can do compared to a long-lived IAM user access key that remains valid indefinitely until manually rotated or deactivated. Best practice treats long-lived access keys as a last resort, reserved for cases where no alternative like an instance role, Lambda execution role, or federated identity is available.

concepts.heading: Common AssumeRole Patterns
concepts.body: Cross-account access, federation with an external IdP, and granting temporary elevated privileges to a human via a 'break-glass' role all rely on the same underlying STS AssumeRole mechanism, differing only in who or what is allowed to call it, which is defined by the target role's trust policy. Session duration, and further permission restriction via an inline session policy passed at assume-time, let you scope a temporary credential even tighter than the role's own permission policy allows.

concepts.heading: Time-Limited Access to Objects with Presigned URLs
concepts.body: A presigned URL grants time-limited access to a single S3 object by embedding a signature generated using the credentials of a principal that already has permission to the object, letting you share a temporary download or upload link with someone who has no AWS credentials of their own, without making the bucket or object public. The URL's validity window is set at generation time and cannot be extended afterward, and revoking access before expiration requires either deleting the object or changing the underlying credentials/policy that authorized the signature.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Authentication Failures
concepts.body: When a user reports they cannot sign in at all, that is an authentication problem, and the investigation starts with CloudTrail's ConsoleLogin events, the identity provider's own sign-in logs (for federated or Cognito users), and IAM Identity Center's session and assignment status, checking for issues like an expired federation certificate, an incorrect SAML assertion, or a misconfigured trust relationship with AWS Directory Service. This differs sharply from a user who can log in fine but is denied when trying to perform a specific action — that is an authorization problem, covered starting in the next lesson.

examPoints: Treat AssumeRole-issued temporary credentials as the default security best practice over long-lived access keys whenever a scenario doesn't explicitly require a static key for an application that has no other way to get credentials.

When a scenario says a user can log in successfully but is then denied access to a specific resource, recognize this immediately as an authorization problem, not an authentication problem, and look toward IAM policy or resource policy answers rather than identity-provider answers.

quiz.q: An application needs to call AWS APIs without embedding any long-lived access keys in its code. Which service issues short-lived, automatically expiring credentials for this purpose?
quiz.explain: STS (Security Token Service) issues temporary security credentials via mechanisms like AssumeRole, which is the standard way to avoid embedding long-lived keys. KMS manages encryption keys and Secrets Manager stores secrets, neither issues temporary AWS API credentials directly the way STS does.

quiz.q: A company wants to let an unauthenticated external partner download one specific file from a private S3 bucket for the next 24 hours only, without making the bucket public.
choices: Creating a new IAM user for the partner
quiz.explain: A presigned URL grants time-limited access to a specific object without exposing the bucket publicly or requiring the partner to have AWS credentials. Making the bucket public would expose all objects, not just the intended one, to everyone.

days.recap: Temporary credentials via STS and presigned URLs minimize the exposure window of any given credential, while authentication troubleshooting starts with CloudTrail sign-in events and is distinct from authorization troubleshooting covered next.

days.title: Authorization Design I: Policies and Trust Relationships

concepts.heading: Fine-Grained Application-Level Authorization
concepts.body: Amazon Verified Permissions is a managed authorization service based on the Cedar policy language that lets an application externalize its own fine-grained, attribute- and role-based access decisions (like 'can this specific user edit this specific document') instead of hardcoding that logic into application code, evaluating policies against a request in real time and returning an allow or deny decision. This is distinct from IAM policies, which govern access to AWS resources and APIs, not to an application's own internal business objects.

concepts.heading: Organizing Identities with IAM Paths
concepts.body: IAM paths let you organize IAM users and roles hierarchically (such as /engineering/backend/) purely for organizational and policy-scoping purposes, which becomes useful when writing permission boundaries or SCPs that need to apply differently based on which part of the organization an identity belongs to, though paths themselves grant no permissions on their own.

concepts.heading: Extending Temporary Credentials to Non-AWS Workloads
concepts.body: IAM Roles Anywhere lets on-premises servers, other clouds, or any workload with an X.509 certificate issued by a trusted certificate authority exchange that certificate for temporary AWS credentials via STS, eliminating the need to provision and rotate long-lived IAM access keys on infrastructure outside AWS. This is the specific answer whenever a scenario describes hybrid or multi-cloud workloads needing AWS access without storing static credentials on infrastructure you don't fully control the security of.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Access via Trust Policies
concepts.body: Granting cross-account access requires two separate authorization checks to succeed: the target role's trust policy (a resource-based policy on the role itself) must name the calling account or principal as an allowed principal, and the calling identity's own permission policy must allow the sts:AssumeRole action against that role's ARN. When cross-account access unexpectedly fails, the systematic check is trust policy first (who can assume this role), then permission policy (is the caller allowed to try), since either one alone is insufficient.

examPoints: When a scenario describes on-premises or non-AWS workloads needing AWS credentials without storing long-lived keys, and mentions X.509 certificates specifically, IAM Roles Anywhere is the answer rather than a generic AssumeRole solution.

When cross-account role assumption fails, remember it requires both sides to agree: the role's trust policy must allow the calling principal, and the caller's own policy must allow calling sts:AssumeRole on that role.

quiz.q: An on-premises data center workload needs to call AWS APIs using X.509 certificates instead of storing long-lived AWS access keys. Which service enables this?
quiz.explain: IAM Roles Anywhere is specifically designed to let on-premises and hybrid workloads exchange X.509 certificates for temporary AWS credentials. Cognito addresses application end-user identity, and Directory Service manages directories, neither handles certificate-based workload authentication.

quiz.q: For a user in Account B to successfully assume a role that exists in Account A, what must the role in Account A have configured?
choices: A trust policy naming Account B (or its principal) as an allowed principal
Account A's root credentials shared with Account B
A VPC peering connection between the accounts
quiz.explain: Cross-account role assumption requires the target role's trust policy to explicitly allow the calling account or principal. Sharing passwords or root credentials is never appropriate, and VPC peering addresses networking, not IAM authorization.

days.recap: Authorization design begins with distinguishing application-level authorization (Verified Permissions) from AWS-resource authorization (IAM policies and trust relationships), and extends AWS's identity model to hybrid workloads via IAM Roles Anywhere.

days.title: Authorization Design II: ABAC, Least Privilege, and Failure Analysis

concepts.heading: Attribute-Based Access Control for Scalable Permissions
concepts.body: ABAC grants or denies access based on matching tags on the principal (such as a department tag on an IAM role) against tags on the resource being accessed, using policy conditions like aws:ResourceTag/department equals aws:PrincipalTag/department, which means a single policy can correctly scope access as new resources and new employees are added, without ever needing to be edited. This contrasts with traditional RBAC, where adding a new resource or team typically requires writing or modifying a dedicated policy, making ABAC the preferred answer whenever a scenario emphasizes a rapidly growing or frequently changing set of resources or users.

concepts.heading: Enforcing Least Privilege with Permission Boundaries and Session Policies
concepts.body: A permission boundary is a managed policy attached to a user or role that sets the maximum permissions that identity (or any role it creates) can ever have, regardless of what its own identity-based policies grant, which is the standard mechanism for letting a delegated administrator create IAM roles for their team without risking those roles ever exceeding an organization-wide ceiling. A session policy, passed as a parameter during AssumeRole, further restricts the resulting temporary credential's permissions below what the role itself allows, useful for scoping down access for one specific, narrow use of a broader role.

concepts.heading: Simulating Policy Evaluation to Diagnose Failures
concepts.body: The IAM Policy Simulator evaluates what a specific principal can and cannot do against specific resources and actions without actually making the API call, which is invaluable for diagnosing why an access-denied error occurs when multiple policies (identity-based, resource-based, permission boundary, SCP) might be interacting in a non-obvious way. Since IAM evaluates an explicit deny in any applicable policy as always winning, the simulator is often the fastest way to find a hidden deny statement, rather than manually re-reading every attached policy.

concepts.heading: Continuous Detection of Unintended External Access
concepts.body: IAM Access Analyzer continuously analyzes resource-based policies (S3 bucket policies, KMS key policies, IAM role trust policies, and others) to identify any that grant access to an external entity outside a defined zone of trust (typically the AWS organization), surfacing these as findings before they become an actual data exposure incident, and it can also generate least-privilege policies based on actual CloudTrail access activity to help tighten overly broad existing permissions. This proactive detection role is distinct from Policy Simulator's reactive, single-principal diagnostic role.

examPoints: When a scenario emphasizes that the set of resources or users keeps growing and rewriting policies for each new one is undesirable, ABAC (tag-based access control) is the intended pattern rather than static RBAC policies.

Distinguish permission boundaries (a ceiling on what an identity or the roles it creates can ever have) from Access Analyzer (detecting unintended external sharing) — both relate to least privilege but solve different problems and are common distractors for each other.

quiz.q: A company's resource count grows constantly, and they want IAM permissions to scope automatically based on matching tags rather than requiring a policy update for every new resource. Which strategy fits?
choices: Using the root account for all access
quiz.explain: ABAC scopes access dynamically based on tags on both the principal and the resource, so growth in resources doesn't require policy changes. Fixed RBAC would require ongoing policy edits as resources are added.

quiz.q: When an IAM user is delegated the ability to create new IAM roles, what mechanism ensures those newly created roles can never exceed a defined maximum set of permissions?
quiz.explain: A permission boundary set on the delegated user (and inherited logic for roles they create) caps the maximum permissions those roles can ever have. Session policies only apply to a single temporary session, not roles created going forward.

days.recap: Authorization design continues with ABAC for scalable, tag-based permissions, permission boundaries and session policies for enforcing least-privilege ceilings, and Policy Simulator plus Access Analyzer for diagnosing and continuously auditing access.

days.title: Domain 4 Review: Authentication vs. Authorization

concepts.heading: The Foundational Split: Who vs. What
concepts.body: Every Domain 4 question ultimately tests one of two questions: 'who is this identity' (authentication — IAM Identity Center, Cognito, MFA, federation, STS) or 'what can this identity do' (authorization — trust policies, ABAC, permission boundaries, Verified Permissions). A scenario describing someone unable to sign in at all is authentication; a scenario describing someone who signs in fine but is denied a specific action is authorization — making this distinction first eliminates half of any answer set immediately.

concepts.heading: Temporary Credentials as the Thread Connecting Both Halves
concepts.body: STS AssumeRole, IAM Roles Anywhere, and Cognito identity pools all solve the same underlying problem — issuing short-lived, scoped credentials instead of long-lived static ones — just for different populations (federated users, hybrid workloads, and application end users respectively). Recognizing this shared pattern helps when a scenario's specific service name is unfamiliar but the underlying need (temporary, least-privilege credentials) is clear.

concepts.heading: Least Privilege as the Organizing Principle for Authorization
concepts.body: ABAC, permission boundaries, session policies, and Access Analyzer are all mechanisms serving the same goal: ensuring an identity has exactly the access it needs and no more, whether that's achieved by dynamic tag matching, a hard ceiling on delegated role creation, a further-restricted temporary session, or continuous detection of unintended external sharing. Treat any Domain 4 question that mentions 'least privilege,' 'over-permissioned,' or 'unintended access' as pointing toward one of these four tools.

concepts.heading: Weighing the Domain Correctly
concepts.body: IAM carries 20% of the exam, the single largest domain, and its concepts (trust policies, least privilege, temporary credentials) recur inside Domain 3 and Domain 6 scenarios as well, so mastery here has an outsized effect on your overall score. Prioritize review time on this domain over any other if time before the exam is limited.

examPoints: Before evaluating any Domain 4 answer choice, classify the question as authentication or authorization first — most wrong answers come from applying an authentication-focused service to an authorization problem or vice versa.

quiz.q: Which statement best distinguishes authentication from authorization?
choices: Authentication confirms who someone is; authorization determines what they can do
Authentication and authorization are the same concept
Authentication is encryption; authorization is logging
Authentication is network security; authorization is data security
quiz.explain: Authentication verifies identity, while authorization determines what actions a verified identity may perform. The other options describe unrelated security concepts, not the authentication/authorization distinction.

quiz.q: Which tool automatically detects IAM resources, such as roles or buckets, that have unintentionally been shared with an entity outside the organization's trust zone?
quiz.explain: IAM Access Analyzer analyzes resource-based policies specifically to identify unintended external sharing. Config Rules check general configuration compliance, CloudTrail records API activity, and Macie classifies data sensitivity — none perform this specific external-access analysis.
